books.section: Topic 4.12 African Americans in the Early Republic, A. Slave Rebellions

primary_sources: Nat Turner, The Confessions of Nat Turner, 1831

stimulus.text:
"And about this time I had a vision—and I saw white spirits and black spirits engaged in battle, and the sun was darkened—the thunder rolled in the heavens, and blood flowed in streams—and I heard a voice saying, “Such is your luck, such you are called to see, and let it come rough or smooth, you must surely bear it.”" — Nat Turner, speaking to Thomas R. Gray, The Confessions of Nat Turner, 1831.

After the rising was put down, Virginia’s legislature debated ending slavery but passed no law, and Southern states tightened the laws governing enslaved people.
stimulus.source_note: Verbatim public-domain quotation from Nat Turner, speaking to Thomas R. Gray, The Confessions of Nat Turner (Baltimore, 1831). Wording checked against the Documenting the American South electronic edition. Aftermath paraphrased from Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 6, Topic 4.12 A, and Princeton Review, Chapter 8.

source: original; stimulus is a verbatim public-domain quotation from Nat Turner (1831)
stem: In the passage, Turner presents his rebellion mainly as

options.text: a plan to seize land for Black farmers
options.misconception: No land plan appears; Turner speaks of spirits and a calling.
Turner speaks of a divine calling, not of a single overseer.

options.text: an escape to the North for himself and his family
options.misconception: Turner stayed to fight; he did not run away.

options.text: a mission God had called him to carry out

rationales.A: Turner never mentions seizing land. He speaks of a vision, spirits, and a voice giving him a task.
rationales.B: No single overseer is named. Turner describes a calling from God, not a personal revenge.
rationales.C: Turner did not flee north. He gathered followers and rose in Southampton County.
rationales.D: Turner says a voice told him what he was called to see and bear. He understood the rising as obedience to God.
rationales.general:
1. Listen to Turner’s words. He speaks of visions, spirits, and a voice giving him a task.
2. Note what is missing. He never mentions land, wages, or escape.
3. Name the frame. Turner understood the rising as obedience to God.
Background: Turner, an enslaved preacher in Southampton County, Virginia, led the rising in August 1831.
Remember: when a writer tells you why he acted, start with his own reason before adding yours.
